steps.observation: Work on this for 30 seconds; do not stop early. How does a transformer neural network work, conceptually?

steps.action:
Conceptual overview of a Transformer neural network

1. Data comes in as discrete tokens  
   • For text, each token is often a wordpiece, sub-word, or character.  
   • Each token is mapped to a continuous vector (an “embedding”) so the model can do math on it.

2. Tokens need a sense of order  
   • Because the architecture has no recurrence, it adds “positional encodings” (sinusoids or learned vectors) to every token embedding.  
   • Now each position carries both its content and its relative place in the sequence.

3. Self-attention: every token looks at every other token  
   • For each position i, the model forms three vectors: a Query qᵢ, a Key kᵢ, and a Value vᵢ (all linear transforms of the embedding).  
   • Attention weights = softmax(qᵢ · kⱼ / √d) for all j.  
   • Those weights say “how much should token i focus on token j?”  
   • The new representation at position i is the weighted sum of all Value vectors vⱼ.  
   • Because this happens in parallel for every i, the model sees global context in one shot.

4. Multi-head trick  
   • Instead of one attention calculation, the model splits the embedding into several smaller subspaces (heads).  
   • Each head learns a different pattern (syntax, long-range coreference, etc.).  
   • Outputs from all heads are concatenated and linearly mixed back together.

5. Local refinement with position-wise feed-forward networks  
   • After attention, each token independently passes through a small two-layer MLP (same weights for all positions).  
   • This lets the model apply nonlinear transformations to the context-aware representations.

6. Stabilizers: residual connections + layer normalization  
   • Residual (skip) connections add the module’s input back to its output, helping gradients flow and preserving information.  
   • Layer norm scales and shifts activations so training is numerically stable.

7. Stacking layers builds depth  
   • One “Transformer block” = multi-head attention + feed-forward, each wrapped in residual + norm.  
   • Stacking many blocks lets later layers reason over increasingly abstract relationships.

8. Output head depends on the task  
   • Language modeling: a linear layer + softmax to predict next-token probabilities.  
   • Classification: reduce sequence to a single vector (e.g., take the [CLS] token) and feed to a classifier.  
   • Sequence-to-sequence (translation, summarization): use an encoder–decoder variant where the decoder attends to encoder outputs.

Why it matters  
• Parallelizable: all positions processed simultaneously, exploiting GPUs better than RNNs.  
• Long-range context: attention lets any token connect to any other in O(n²) operations, so distant dependencies are learned easily.  
• Modularity: by tweaking attention masks (e.g., causal masking), the same core design supports many tasks from autoregressive text generation to bidirectional encoders like BERT.

High-level intuition  
Think of self-attention as a dynamic “word-to-word searchlight.” Each word decides—on the fly—how much to borrow information from every other word, and multiple heads let these searchlights capture different perspectives. The feed-forward sublayer then refines these richer token states. Stacking dozens of such layers yields powerful representations that underpin today’s state-of-the-art models in NLP and beyond.
